17         Plaintiff Cynthia Hays (“Plaintiff”), on behalf of herself and all others similarly situated, asserts
18 that following against Defendant LinkedIn Corporation (“LinkedIn” or “Defendant”), based upon

19 personal knowledge, where applicable, information and belief, and the investigation of counsel:

20                                       NATURE OF THE ACTION
21         1.      Plaintiff brings this case to address Defendant’s unlawful practice of intercepting
22 Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ confidential personal health communications with Covered California,

23 without their knowledge or consent.

24         2.      LinkedIn is a social networking site that is predominately used for professional
25 networking and career development.

26         3.      Like other social networking platforms—such as Facebook, Snapchat, and TikTok—
27 LinkedIn offers website operators, such as Covered California, a tracking technology that can be

28 embedded on a website to collect and analyze how individuals interact with a given website.

 1          4.      LinkedIn’s tracking technology—the LinkedIn Insight Tag (“Insight Tag”)—is a snippet

 2 of JavaScript computer code embedded on a third-party website that tracks a visitor’s actions as they

 3 navigate through the website. It logs the URLs of pages they visit, the buttons they click, their IP address,

 4 and more. 1 This information is collected in real time and sent to LinkedIn who then utilizes the harvested

 5 data to target individuals with advertisements on its social media platform.

 6          5.      LinkedIn profits from this large-scale data collection. The Insight Tag is marketed

 7 towards businesses that use LinkedIn Ads as a way to “optimize” their advertising campaigns and

 8 LinkedIn generates substantial revenue through its advertising services. 2

 9          6.      These benefits appeal to website operators, with over 150,000 websites in the United
10 States utilizing the Insight Tag. 3

11          7.      Recently, it was discovered that the Insight Tag was embedded on Covered California’s

12 website, https://www.coveredca.com/, the organization that lets Californians shop for health insurance

13 under the Affordable Care Act. 4

14          8.      When a visitor to https://www.coveredca.com/ shopped for health insurance, the Insight

15 Tag intercepted sensitive health information, and sent that information to LinkedIn, providing Defendant

16 with intimate personal facts and data in the form of their sensitive health information.

17          9.      The intercepted data included information from forms website visitors filled out,

18 including sensitive health information such as whether they were blind, pregnant, or used prescription

19 medication; along with information about visitor’s ethnicity or marital status. The Insight Tag also

20 captured information about visitors’ doctors and specialties if they selected doctors covered by a specific

21 health plan offered through Covered California. 5

 1                                      FACTUAL BACKGROUND

 2          19.    Covered California is California’s health insurance marketplace that was established

 3 under the Affordable Care Act to help Californian’s find and afford health insurance plans. Over 1.9

 4 million individuals have enrolled in health insurance through Covered California. 6

 5          20.    Covered California operates the website and subpages of coveredca.com, which allows

 6 Californias to shop for and compare health insurance plans.

 7          21.    Unbeknownst to Californians shopping for health insurance on coveredca.com, however,

 8 the Insight Tag was embedded on coveredca.com and its subpages, collecting information Californians

 9 submitted to Covered California.
10          22.    Indeed, a recent investigation by The Markup revealed that between February 2024 and
11 April 2025, the Insight Tag was tracking visitors coveredca.com and disclosing their health information

12 submitted to Covered California to LinkedIn. 7

13          A.     How LinkedIn’s Insight Tags Work

14          23.    Web browsers are software applications that allow consumers to navigate the internet and

15 view and exchange electronic information and communications. Each “client device” (such as computer,

16 tablet, or smart phone) accessed web content through a web browser (e.g., Google’s Chrome browser,

17 Mozilla’s Firefox browser, Apple’s Safari browser, and Microsoft’s Edge browser).

18          24.    Every website is hosted by a computer “server” that holds the website’s contents and

19 through which the website owner exchanges files or communications with Internet users’ client devices

20 via their web browsers.

21          25.    Web communications consist of HTTP or HTTPS Requests and HTTP or HTTPS

22 Responses. Any given browsing session may consist of thousands of individual HTTP Requests and

23 HTTP Responses, along with corresponding cookies:

 1          •     HTTP Request: an electronic communication sent from the client device’s browser to the
 2                website’s server. GET Requests are one of the most common types of HTTP Requests. In

 3                addition to specifying a particular URL (i.e., web address), GET Requests can also send data

 4                to the host server embedded inside the URL, and can include cookies. POST Requests are a

 5                separate type of HTTP Request that can send a large amount of data outside of the URL (e.g.,

 6                uploading a PDF to a court’s ECF system for filing a motion).

 7          •     Cookies: a small text file that can be used to store information on the client device which can
 8                later be communicated to a server or servers. Cookies that have been placed on the client

 9                device are sent with HTTP Requests from client devices to the host server. Some cookies are

10                “third-party cookies” which means they can store and communicate data to the cookie
11                owner’s website when the user is visiting an entirely different website.
12          •     HTTP Response: an electronic communication that is sent as a reply to the client device’s
13                web browser from the host server in response to an HTTP Request. HTTP Responses may
14                consist of a web page, another kind of file, text information, or error codes, among other data.
15                HTTP Responses can also send cookies or other code hidden and embedded in the webpage
16                to the client device’s browser.
17          26.      When an individual visits Covered California’s website, an HTTP Request is sent from
18 that individual’s web browser to Covered California’s servers that asks the website to retrieve certain

19 information. The HTTP Response from Covered California’s servers sends the requested information in

20 the form of “Markup.” This is the foundation for the pages, images, words, buttons, and other features

21 that appear on the visitor’s screen as they navigate the website.

22          27.      Every website is comprised of Markup and “Source Code.” Source Code is simply a set
23 of instructions that commands the website visitor’s browser to take certain actions when the web page

24 first loads or when a specified event triggers the code.

25          28.      Source code may also command a web browser to send data transmissions to third parties

26 in the form of HTTP Requests quietly executed in the background without notifying the web browser’s

27 user. Defendant’s Insight Tag is source code that does just that, and acts much like a traditional wiretap.

28 When members visit Covered California website via an HTTP Request to Covered California’s server,

                                                    5
                                         CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT

 1 Covered California’s server sends an HTTP Response including the Markup that displays the Webpage

 2 visible to the user along with Source Code that includes Defendant’s Insight Tags. Once the Webpage

 3 loads in the members browser, Defendant’s Insight Tags quietly wait for a communication from the

 4 member to trigger the tag, which intercepts those communications intended only for Covered California

 5 and delivers the content of those communications to Defendant.

 6          29.    Insight Tags manipulate the web users’ browser by secretly instructing it to duplicate the

 7 members’ communications (HTTP Requests) with Covered California and to send those

 8 communications to LinkedIn. These transmissions occur contemporaneously, invisibly, and without the

 9 user’s knowledge.
10          30.    The Insight Tags are programmed to automatically track and transmit communications
11 made between Covered California and its users. The Insight Tags execute instructions that effectively

12 open a hidden spying window into the patient’s browser through which LinkedIn can intercept the

13 visitor’s data, actions, and communications with Covered California.

14          31.    The user visiting Covered California only sees the Markup, not Defendant’s Insight Tags
15 or the underlying HTTP Requests and Responses.

16          32.    The inclusion of Insight Tags on a website does not provide any substantive content to
17 the website user. In other words, LinkedIn does not provide anything to the user, but only serves to track

18 user data and communications to further the marketing purposes of the website owner (i.e., to bolster

19 profits).

20          33.    Thus, without any knowledge, authorization, or action by a user, LinkedIn uses its Insight
21 Tag source code to commandeer the computing devices of Covered California users, causing the

22 device’s web browser to contemporaneously and invisibly re-direct communications to LinkedIn.

23          34.    In this case, LinkedIn intercepted Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ Personal Health
24 Information to acquire data to power its targeted advertising business.

25          35.    Consequently, when Plaintiff and Class Members visit Covered California and
26 communicated their Personal Health Information, including, but not limited to, precise text of search

27 queries about specific doctors and prescription drugs; users’ downloads of information about specific

 1 illnesses, conditions, and mental health disorders; summaries of communications between patients and

 2 Covered California; these communications are simultaneously intercepted and transmitted to LinkedIn.

 3          36.     LinkedIn tracks internet users with IP addresses, cookies, geolocation, and other unique

 4 device identifiers.

 5          37.     LinkedIn also uses personally identifiable cookies, such as “li_at” and “li_rm,” which

 6 contain digitally signed and encrypted records of a user’s LinkedIn account.

 7          38.     LinkedIn uses cookies like li_at and li_rm to help customize ads on LinkedIn. For

 8 example, LinkedIn uses such cookies to remember users’ most recent searches, previous interactions

 9 with an advertiser’s ads or search results, and visits to an advertiser’s website. This helps LinkedIn show
10 customized ads to users on LinkedIn.

11          39.     LinkedIn cookies thus provide personally identifiable data about patients who visit
12 Covered California’s website, and LinkedIn intercepts this information for its targeted advertising

13 purposes.

10           93.   18 U.S.C. § 2520(a) provides a private right of action to any person whose wire or
11 electronic communications are intercepted, disclosed, or intentionally used in violation of the ECPA.

12           94.   The ECPA protects both sending and receipt of communications.
13           95.   Electronic Communications. The transmission of Personal Health Information between
14 Plaintiff and Class Members and Covered California via its Website are “transfer[s] of signs, signals,

15 writing,…data, [and] intelligence of [some] nature transmitted in whole or in part by a wire, radio,

16 electromagnetic, photoelectronic, or photooptical system that affects interstate commerce” and are

17 therefore “electronic communications” within the meaning of 18 U.S.C. § 2510(12).

18           96.   Content. The ECPA defines content, when used with respect to electronic
19 communications, to “include[] any information concerning the substance, purport, or meaning of that

20 communication.” 18 U.S.C. § 2510(8). The contents of Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ communications

21 include, but are not limited to, IP addresses, LinkedIn cookies containing user account information,

22 URLs, file downloads, and the text of search queries, all of which concern substance and meaning of

23 Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ personal identities and protected health information such as medical

24 conditions, prescriptions, and treatment.

25           97.   Interception. The ECPA defines the interception as the “acquisition of the contents of
26 any wire, electronic, or oral communication through the use of any electronic, mechanical, or other

27 device” and “contents … include any information concerning the substance, purport, or meaning of that

28 communication.” 18 U.S.C. § 2510(4), (8). Whenever Plaintiff and Class Members interacted with
